Joseph Erwin (1762 – April 14, 1829) was an American racehorse owner, owner of cotton and sugar plantations, and a slave trader. Their conflict over their competing thoroughbred racehorses, Erwin's Ploughboy and Jackson's Truxton, led to the fatal 1806 duel between Jackson and Erwin's son-in-law Charles Dickinson.

The whole life of Joseph Erwin reads like a single decision repeated. After Dickinson's death at Jackson's hand, Erwin moved to Louisiana where he owned as many as seven plantations and hundreds of slaves. Joseph Erwin was born to Robert and Martha Erwin in 1761 in Guilford County, British North Carolina.

Between the birth and the legend of Joseph Erwin lie the years that actually decide it. In 1782 there was a marriage bond filed for Joseph Erwin and "Livy McMamey" in Guilford County. Erwin's bondsman and witness was land speculator David Allison. "Livy McMamey" was born Lavinia Thompson; her first husband had been a man named James McKemey.

The reputation of Joseph Erwin was built in the middle, not at the edges. Lavinia Thompson's brother Jason Thompson married Catherine McNairy, a sister of John McNairy, Nathaniel McNairy, and Boyd McNairy. After he arrived in the Nashville area in the 1790s he began growing cotton on what was called Peach Blossom plantation.

Somebody like Joseph Erwin should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. In 1797 he bought 540 acres of land near Richland Creek that had been part of the North Carolina military land grant of Francis Hodge. In 1800 he bought another 100 acres of Hodge's grant, and then in 1805 he added another 50 acres, purchased from James Martin, to the property that eventually became known as the Haynes place.

The life of Joseph Erwin begins far from where the story usually starts. Originally a brick Georgian-style mansion with a drive that fronted on what became the Richland Turnpike (West End Ave), Peach Blossom was surrounded by 650 acres. He was a very wealthy man, having large sugar plantations at Plaquemines, La., though he resided in Tennessee.

The legacy of Joseph Erwin outlived the circumstances that produced it. To summarize, Joseph Erwin owned a horse named Tanner that lost a race to Greyhound, a horse owned by Jackson. Erwin wanted a rematch of sorts, with his horse Ploughboy racing against Jackson's Truxton.

Few lives travel as far as that of Joseph Erwin, and the distance is the point. The race was planned for November 28, 1805, with a $2,000 purse, but Erwin withdrew Ploughboy before the race, and paid the agreed-upon $800 forfeit fee. There was a disagreement about which type of "note" (cash equivalent) would be used to pay the fee, but it was resolved and Jackson got paid.

The childhood of Joseph Erwin contains the adult in small print. After that, there was a long run of masculine posturing, snippy newspaper columns, hostile letters, and all manner of 1805 Tennessee interpersonal drama, including an episode where Jackson caned a man in a tavern because he was not a good enough "gentleman" to be worth dueling. Things escalated, a duel challenge was issued, the two Tennesseans stepped over to Kentucky so as to not violate their state's anti-dueling laws, and a duel was fought.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Joseph Erwin — in that order. The turning point in the life of Joseph Erwin looked like a failure at the time. Erwin was administrator of his son-in-law's estate and placed a newspaper ad stating that on January 12, 1808, he would be hiring out Dickinson's estate slaves for a 12-month term. In 1807, Joseph Erwin and his wife relocated to Iberville Parish, Territory of Orleans, where they established a plantation just below Plaquemine.

Every biography of Joseph Erwin has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. The plantation was purchased from Nicholas Rousseau and consisted of five and a half arpents of land along the river, just below the confluence of the river and Bayou Plaquemine. In 1807 he had a trunk stolen at the Natchez, Mississippi boat landing containing six weeks worth of "bills of sale for negroes" and 50-odd promissory notes totaling US$20,000 (equivalent to $439,773 in 2025).

The following month they placed a similar ad in a Nashville newspaper, stating that the total value of the notes was approximately US$20,000 (equivalent to $439,773 in 2025), and that they were all dated to between March 24 and May 4, 1807.

What Joseph Erwin wanted at the start and what Joseph Erwin got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Erwin paid US$10,000 (equivalent to $219,886 in 2025) for his first plantation in June 1807. Over the next 20 years he bought and sold 30,000 arpents of plantation land, with his holdings running miles along the riverfront.

The defining trait of Joseph Erwin was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. The plantations were primarily planted in cotton and provisions; some of the land was put in sugarcane starting in the 1820s. In 1808, Erwin, Spraggins & Wright offered a $100 reward for the capture of 24-year-old Jacob and 21-year-old Job, who had been enslaved by them near the Bayou Plaquemines, Iberville Parish, Orleans Territory.

Those who met Joseph Erwin at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. The private years of Joseph Erwin explain the public decades better than any speech. By 1817 Erwin had raised his reward rate to $20 per slave and was looking to recover 30-year-old Tom who was tall, had a "yellow complexion" and a limp, and as well as a "yellow fellow" in his early 20s named Jim. In 1822 Erwin, in partnership with brothers George and Robert Bell, bought 93 slaves from Warner Washington II of Virginia, a cousin of George Washington.

The family Joseph Erwin came from matters more than the legends admit. The US$34,000 (equivalent to $822,375 in 2025) purchase was made with a cash down payment and debt financing of the remainder, due in 1828, 1829, and 1830. The debt was guaranteed by a mortgage on Erwin's Louisiana land, and the mortgage eventually came into the hands of Lawrence Lewis, who later granted the same instrument to his daughter, wife of Andrew Jackson's former ward Edward G.

The first real success of Joseph Erwin arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. In 1824, someone stole another Erwin promissory note, this one being an exchange between Joseph Erwin to John Erwin, in the amount of US$3,250 (equivalent to $95,284 in 2025). As early as 1825, family friends began to describe Erwin as "mentally imbalanced, drinking heavily, and in financial distress." Erwin had apparently experienced financial reversals as a result of the Panic of 1819.

The last chapter of Joseph Erwin was written long after the fame. Mississippi River flooding of the Home Place and Evergreen Plantations in 1828 resulted in a loss of income. The total value of his estate was appraised at US$368,000 (equivalent to $11,126,250 in 2025).

The whole life of Joseph Erwin reads like a single decision repeated. In a fit of mental derangement (of which the deceased had of late been subject) as is supposed, he enveloped his head in a blanket, and plunged into a large water jar, head foremost, in which situation he was found lifeless. Slave prices were high in the year 1818, and records show Erwin sold US$19,000 (equivalent to $399,620 in 2025) worth of people that year.

Between the birth and the legend of Joseph Erwin lie the years that actually decide it. Newton Cannon, a nephew of Erwin, was later elected governor of Tennessee. Newton Cannon's mother and Erwin's wife are believed to have both been daughters of Robert Thompson of Guilford County, North Carolina, who was killed at the Battle of Alamance in 1771.
